utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. It's Matthew Olmsted, Joanna Korner, Crispian Smith, and our intern, Tatjana Quast with us today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we continue with the examination-in-chief of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may be seated, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we continue with the examination-in-chief of Mr. Radulovic, there are two small preliminary matters which the Trial Chamber wishes to raise. One is that on Friday the OTP, and in person Ms. Korner, had invited us to reconsider the ruling that we had given excluding the number of articles written and published by the Witness Traynor, and indicating that -- presumably taking on board the reservations that the Chamber had expressed, indicated that the application would have been modified - that's my choice of words, not necessarily what she had said - limiting it to the articles to which he specifically spoke during his testimony. We think that we are inclined to accede to that application, but for the purpose of clarity, we would need, in the course of today, hopefully, or at the earliest convenience of the OTP, the articles in question. We have the full list that the -- with which we had been provided; but we need, in order to rule, to know precisely which articles it is that Ms. Korner had in mind on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say, I had them actually yesterday, but it didn't seem appropriate to raise them. I can provide the numbers at the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. The second matter is that it would be recalled that yesterday we had given an oral ruling in respect of an application which the OTP had made on the 18th of May dealing with the addition of three items to their 65 ter list, and we had given a partial ruling, the Defence not objecting, in respect of two of those items because they dealt with the witness who is presently on the stand. There is a remaining item. The 65 ter number would be 3598. And subject to being persuaded to the contrary by the Defence, we would similarly be inclined to admit that -- allow the inclusion of that item, although we appreciate that the relevant witness isn't scheduled to appear before July. So if the Defence, and as I said, accepting that, as we indicated yesterday, you can make the argument about time, but that apart, that we would wish to hear from the Defence before we formally rule on the admission -- on the inclusion of this 3598. Thank you. Mr. Radulovic, before Mr. Olmsted continues his examination-in-chief, I remind you you're still on you oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have on the screen P1373, which was admitted at the end of the session yesterday. And if we could turn to page 2 of the B/C/S and page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: First of all, good morning, Mr. Radulovic.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We took a look at this document at the end of the day yesterday, and I just want to ask you a couple more questions about it. You can see that this is -- as we discussed before, this is a SNB Banja Luka payroll for June 1992. And if you can look at number 12 on this list, we see the name "Zdravko Samardzija."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Maybe we can zoom in on number 12 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you see that name there, Mr. Radulovic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's kind of illegible, but I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the last page of this document, both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see, on this page -- I'll wait for the B/C/S to come up. We see on this page the first name on the list is Ljuban Ecim. Mr. Radulovic, does this mean that Samardzija and Ecim remained with SNB Banja Luka while they were with the Banja Luka Special Police Detachment?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know. And, throughout, they were on the list as staff of the SNB. There was a remark that they were temporarily deployed to another unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How would you describe the relationship -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphone of the accused please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what kind of relationship you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I was interrupted with my question. Could you describe the relationship between Mr. Zupljanin and the special police detachment commanders?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing special. I only know that the special detachment was part of the CSB and, frankly speaking, I know that Ljuban Ecim was much closer to Mr. Nedeljko Kesic than he was to Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, with whom he didn't have such close ties. That is my personal observation, and I believe that the events that ensued after 1992 corroborate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us how closely Mr. Zupljanin followed the activities of the CSB police detachment?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know to what extent he followed it, but I believe that the detachment had more contacts and closer ties to the SDB than the SJB, regardless of subordination, the command, and everything else, because the managerial staff -- the commanding staff of that detachment belonged to the SNB, and I believe that is the reason why this detachment was so close to the SNB not only at the level of Banja Luka, but also at the level of the entire republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, was Mr. Zupljanin aware of the activities of the special police detachment, their observations in the field?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Mr. Stojan Zupljanin for the first time in person when I first went to Doboj, because I had received information and I also saw with my own eyes what that detachment was doing in Doboj. After returning from Doboj, I immediately informed Mr. Stojan Zupljanin in person that the members of the SNB, who were treated as a special unit and they were conspicuous because they wore special hats and they were called the hat-bearers, they committed serious crimes, and I suggested to the chief, Mr. Zupljanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. I apologise, but I want to focus you on my questions today, because we don't have enough time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, let him finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: He's not being responsive to my question. My question is not about crimes of the special police at this point; it's just generally did Mr. Zupljanin follow the operations of the special police detachment when they went out in the field to conduct an operation. Whatever they did in the field is not what I'm asking for right now, but whether he followed the operations, as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It would be helpful if the witness would confine himself to answering the specific questions that is asked. But inasmuch as this seems to be -- this is not an irrelevant point, and it's a point which Mr. Krgovic apparently is interested in, lest it be -- while it's live, perhaps the witness should be permitted to continue, and then you can return to your question, Mr. -- if it needs to be repeated, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, we will be -- we will be asking questions about this particular incident in Doboj a little bit later, and so I'm just trying to avoid repeating ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But at any rate, Mr. Zupljanin [sic], I'm sorry for interrupting you. Can you please finish what you were saying, and then we'll focus back on my question. I'm sorry. Mr. Radulovic, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I? I had the feeling -- that was my first oral report to the chief, Mr. Zupljanin. I had a feeling that he was surprised, that he couldn't believe that the members of the special detachment from Banja Luka were doing that. He said he would check. On the following day, I didn't know what Mr. Zupljanin had done, but on the day after that, in other words, on the third day after the event, I saw that the members of the special detachment were withdrawing from Doboj to Banja Luka, and that withdrawal of theirs was not short because they were taking with them what they had taken or looted in the area of Doboj. As I knew some people who were members of that special detachment, I saw an incredible lot of valuable things that they had looted in Doboj. From that, I drew the conclusion that Stojan Zupljanin had taken some steps to withdraw our detachment from Doboj, considering the fact that local criminals also committed crimes using the presence of this other group as a front, and they attributed their own deeds to them. I don't know whether this will suffice for you, but this was the impression I got; namely, that Stojan Zupljanin, when I first informed him, didn't have true information about the activities of the special detachment in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when you had this discussion with Mr. Zupljanin about the special police detachment?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special police detachment, before my report, had been present in Doboj for about two weeks. I remember well that I received the first information from collaborators from the Doboj area. I learned that crimes were being committed there. I admit that at first I couldn't believe that such crimes were being committed, and when I went to Doboj and saw -- and talked to various collaborators and operative connections, as well as members of the public security and state security, with whom I was on good terms and heard from them what was happening in Doboj, you can believe me that to me this was the first information -- the first unpleasant information that I received that this was done by members of my people and members of the service to which I belonged. Those people were doing that freely, without anybody in Doboj doing anything to prevent them. I must remind you that it was especially difficult for me when I learned in Doboj that the mistreatment and -- or, rather, that even people with whom I had long worked in Doboj such as Karlo Grgic or Professor Dr. Ilija Tipura had been mistreated or killed. Many other people, too, came to harm from these individuals. Some were killed and some died as a consequence of mistreatment. This was why I suggested to the managerial staff of the SJB, among them Mr. Zupljanin, that we must do everything to protect the members of the SJB to -- so that they aren't harmed by these criminals and renegades. And, if it is their wish, to allow them to leave the RS freely with all their valuables, without being searched, without anything being taken away from them, without them being mistreated. And I must say that fortunately it was a common position that every -- or every one of these workers, including the SJB and the SDB, being able to do so. And it was, indeed, done. I don't know what else might interest you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Why don't we take a look at P1337.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I would like you to insist a little bit on your initial question; not the crimes, not Mr. Zupljanin's knowledge about the crimes, but Mr. Zupljanin's place in the chain of command, what -- you know, that you initially wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, but since we've opened up this topic of this Doboj incident, I think I'll cover this first and then go back to that, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very good. If we could look at P1337. And perhaps we can just quickly turn to the second page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, can you confirm that this is one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This report is dated 17 May 1992 and discusses or reports events in Doboj around that time-period. And in the first paragraph - if we can turn to the first page - it reports on crimes committed against the non-Serb population in Doboj and attributes these crimes to special forces from Banja Luka and special forces organised by a man called Bozovic. First of all, is this around the time that you had this discussion with Zupljanin about the activities of the special police detachment?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. At that time, I can't remember the exact date, but what you're mentioning with regard to this, Bozovic was not a member of the Banja Luka Special Detachment. He was from Belgrade, Serbia, and as far as I know, he was in the Doboj region to train special forces members from Doboj to become eligible for members of the special forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you provide us with the first name of Mr. Bozovic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Radoman Bozovic. I know that his roots are in Montenegro. I met him two or three times. I informed the man of the activities of those who were using the Red Berets as a front, and I know what his reaction was. At the time, he stepped on an anti-personnel mine, and he was taken away on a stretcher. I know that he beat those who were committing crimes even as he lay there on the stretcher. He was holding an automatic rifle by the barrel, and he threatened them that they would be killed, even. And he said to them, Are you the so-called Serb fighters? You call yourselves Serb heroes and do such things. I must say that because it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for that. But please -- please try to limit your answers to my question, because I think my question was simply whether this report, which is dated 17 May 1992, was around the time you had the discussion with Mr. Zupljanin, and you've given us substantially more than that. So please try to keep your answers short. You referred to, in this report, the special forces from Banja Luka. Is that the special police detachment from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who was leading that detachment at this time?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who was the number-one man in Doboj when I went there. It was Ljuban Ecim. There was also Zdravko Samardzija, and I need not repeat all the names that I have already mentioned here; the entire group, the Kojic brothers, Subara, and so on. They're all identified in my reports with their full names, so I don't need to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned Bozovic. And you said his first name was, I think, Radomir. Was it Radomir or Radojica?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radojica, well, where I'm from, names are frequently changed, such as Radoman into Radovan. I'm not quite sure, but he may have been either Radomir or Radojica Bozovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to further clarify, you mentioned the Red Berets. Was that the name of the group that was under him?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you describe, in this report, a number of crimes committed against the non-Serb population, and then earlier in your testimony you mentioned the mistreatment and killing of some, I believe, former police officers who were non-Serbs. Can you tell us what other crimes they were committing against non-Serbs in Doboj around this time?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to say that in a nutshell. All kinds of crime; rape, mistreatment, murder, looting, anything. If I give you an example, I think it will do. At the entrance to the CSB, I was stopped by an old, experienced police officer by the name of Mile Bosnjak. He was like in a trance. He recognised me because I had worked in Doboj before, and he used to call every employee of his service whom he met in civilian clothes "Boss." So he told me, Boss, I'll kill myself. And I said, What's happening? I thought he was pulling my leg. And then he told me about an experience of his. The members of these paramilitary units, or whatever you may choose to call them, four of them raped a 13-year-old girl in front of her mother in one of the residential high-rise buildings in Doboj. At the time, my daughters were about that age, and, of course, I was unable to control myself, being very emotional, and I asked who had done it. And he told me, among others, that the hat-bearers were doing that together with the local criminals. Having learned that Karlo Grgic had been killed, a man I knew, a professional -- he was the commander of the police station in Doboj, then Ilija Tipura, he was a doctor of legal science and a professor, and he was also chief of the CSB before the war, so knowing who had been killed, of the people I knew, and who had been mistreated -- among others, they even mistreated the family that looked after my children while I lived in Doboj. And it wasn't merely mental harassment, but also physical mistreatment by locking them up in some private or semi-private detention rooms or prisons or whatever. So whatever was -- whoever was found on the street and recognised as being non-Serbian was taken away and mistreated horribly. On the same day, I met Andrija Bjelosevic, and I wanted to know what the problem was. Andrija Bjelosevic was the chief of the service in Doboj, and I remember that in his office I met my earlier chief of the inter-municipal SUP, Milan Maric. It was a convenient moment because Milan Maric was one of the professionals with the greatest experience in Yugoslavia; everybody knew them, every professional. And I asked Andrija Bjelosevic to put an end to it, and he told me, literally, I can do nothing about it. Because they are local groups - if you want, I can mention who it was - local criminals who are stronger than the SJB and the SDB because they enjoy the support of political circles. And I said, Who? And he said, Drago Paravac. And I went to Drago Paravac right away because his office was in the building across the street from the SUP. And I met a man whom I had known before, and I said -- I think at the time he was president of the Executive Committee of Doboj. I told him -- well, I didn't call him sir because I rarely say sir to anybody, and I asked, What's happening in Doboj? And it was -- he told me, But what? What's the problem? As if it was a theatre performance. And I said, Man, come on, can't you see that crimes are being committed? They are bringing in Croats and Bosniaks on buses. Because there was a detention facility, a prison of sorts. They are being beaten up and mistreated. And he told me, So what? And I said, Man, but can't you understand what this is about? And he was looking at me as if I were from outer space or something, as if I were talking about irrelevant things, about trifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I might interrupt. There are two observations that I would make. One is that I think you're going a little too quickly for the interpreters, so you need to slow down a bit. But, secondly, we appreciate that you are a witness to certain events, and it is in the context of your -- what you would have observed that you have been asked to attend as a witness. But the -- in order for a trial before this Tribunal or, indeed, any tribunal anywhere in the world to move forward in a way that the decision-makers, in this case the Judges, at the end of the day can do their work, it is not the best way to have a witness just give a narrative. The reason why counsel on either side are present is that understanding what the charges are with which the Trial Chamber is concerned, that is, what is specified in the indictment, counsel for the Prosecution, on the one hand, and for the Defence, on the other, would have, in terms of the questions which they intend to ask, a sort of road map as to where to lead, so that not -- whereas the questions that counsel asks, you are expected to answer out of the context of what you observed. It is not an invitation for you to continue a narrative, if you understand what I'm saying. So, in other words, one of the difficulties that we are experiencing is that when counsel asks a question, we expect that the answer that the witness would give would relate to that question, so that we, as the Judges, can follow where counsel is leading us. And the same thing would arise when we hear from -- when counsel from the other side asks you questions. So bearing that in mind, if you would listen to the question that counsel asks and only answer that question, then it would be of benefit to all of us, yourself included. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you and I respect you, but I understood the question of the Prosecutor to mean that he wanted to know what crimes were committed in Doboj. I didn't know how else to describe it, other than to give them a picture of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned hat-bearers. Who were the hat-bearers? Just remind us who they were.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the umpteenth time, the hat-bearers were members of the special police detachment from Banja Luka. I can tell you that in Doboj they were in a platoon, which means that there were about 30 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you also mentioned two individuals, Karlo Grgic and Ilija Tipura. Can you tell us what their ethnicities were?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of them were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you've described for us a number of crimes occurring in Doboj in this month of May. Did you inform -- when you had this conversation with Mr. Zupljanin, did you inform him about all these different types of crimes that the special police detachment and other units in Doboj were committing?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed them in general terms about the crimes, about the crimes that were being committed, and I told them that unfortunately members of the special police detachment from Banja Luka participated in those crimes as well. And two or three days later, the members of the special detachment were withdrawn, were pulled out from Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were any measures taken to discipline or criminally charge the special police detachment members for any of the crimes they committed in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a quick look at 65 ter 10187.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- I was just reminded by my colleague that in your witness statement you mentioned that they were pulled out -- the special police detachment was pulled out in June of 1992. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning -- in the beginning of June or in late May. I can't be more specific than that as to the date, but at around that time, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, is this one of your reports? Wait, hold on a second. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We have a technical problem here. We have the wrong B/C/S version on the screen. It doesn't match the English translation. So I'm going to come back to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, you mentioned that it was Mr. Zupljanin who withdrew the special police detachment from Doboj at the end of May or beginning of June. Does this mean that Mr. Zupljanin was the ultimate commander of the special police detachment, at least during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Objection. It's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, then, can you elaborate further on Mr. Zupljanin's powers over this special police detachment?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Let me just say that after I informed them verbally, the special detachment was withdrawn from Doboj, and I understood that the special detachment had been withdrawn on the order of Stojan Zupljanin. That was my understanding. And I think that he did have certain powers -- or, rather, among other things, he was also authorised to command that unit. Now, whether he did it directly or whether via his subordinates, right now I simply don't know that, and at the time it wasn't really something that I would inquire about. What was important was that people were withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Where else, other than Doboj, did the special police detachment conduct operations in 1992, let's say between April and September 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, I know that for a while some of them were stationed in Kotor Varos. They behaved the same or similarly to how they behaved in Doboj. I know that everybody had problems with them. And it was the leadership of Kotor Varos that had the most problems with them because they imposed themselves as the lords. They subjugated everything to themselves, and they refused to co-ordinate and co-operate with any organs or authorities in the Kotor Varos area at the local level. They committed crimes. Now, if you're interested in what kind of crimes, I can tell you that, too, because I wrote about that. And naturally they went to other areas very frequently, such as Prijedor, Kljuc. And please don't ask me to speak about Kljuc, since I will appear as Defence witness [as interpreted] in the Kljuc case, and it wouldn't be proper and it could also be unlawful for me to testify about Kljuc here. So please don't put any questions about Kljuc to me, but you can ask me about Prijedor and about their activities there in Kotor Varos and so on. As for their participation in operations at the front-line, I don't know much about that. I don't know anything specific that might be of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that we have here in transcript - it's page 17 -- it's page 17, line 4 - in response there is a word "Defence witness." It is not what witness actually said. So please, Mr. Olmsted, clarify that with him, in which capacity he is mentioned -- acting, and he's mentioning this case before a Sarajevo court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, just for clarification for the record, we have it, in the English transcript, that you said you were a Defence witness in the Kljuc case. Are you, in fact, a Defence counsel in the Kljuc case?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm Defence counsel in that case, one of Defence counsel in that case before the BH Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And I do apologise. And could we have a name of the client and function of the client, so just for the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I don't think that's relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, you've mentioned that the special police detachment were in Kotor Varos, Prijedor, and you mentioned Kljuc. We won't talk about that. But was this after they had conducted this operation in Doboj, so after May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And to your knowledge and based on your intelligence information, was Mr. Zupljanin aware of the operations that his detachment were conducting in these other municipalities, Kotor Varos, Kljuc, and Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that it was you who put to me various dispatches and information notes that I wrote at the time, one can see from those documents that I informed my immediate superior, Vojin Bera, and I also informed orally Nedeljko Kesic. Now, as to whether those information notes and dispatches ever reached Stojan Zupljanin, I truly don't know that. I had occasion once, or maybe more than once - two or three times - to talk to Mr. Zupljanin about what was going on in the Prijedor and Kotor Varos area, and among other things I mentioned the activities of the members of the special detachment of the SJB, or whatever they were called. So I did inform him. And I know, on the basis of contacts with him, that he also expressed certain concern in relation to their behaviour in Kotor Varos and in Prijedor. I remember - I don't know if he still remembers - that he used to tell me that he received similar information from local leadership; first of all, the chief in Kotor Varos. And I know that there was a worker of ours who worked there, Zdravko Pejic. He was from the State Security Service. And based on what I know, he also sent information about crimes committed by members of the special detachment in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And let me just clarify. The special police detachment was in Kotor Varos after its operations in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take look at 2D72. And if we can turn to page 20 of the B/C/S and page 23 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have before us is an official ID that's of the special police detachment, and it's for an individual by the name of Miroslav Dragojevic. Have you ever seen this kind of identification card before?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, hundreds of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is this the identification card that the special police detachment members would carry?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were supposed to have it on them always when on assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And whose signature appears on this card?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that it's a signature of Zupljanin, which corroborates something I have said earlier; namely, that according to what I know, the special police detachment was subordinated to the chief of the security services of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page in the B/C/S and stay where we are in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is the back of the card, and it authorises the special police member to enter other people's apartments and premises, stay there, and perform searches without an order from the relevant organ. Mr. Radulovic, did the special police conduct searches of non-Serb apartments and premises without court orders in 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of a single case where there was a court order, and I know of a lot of cases where searches were conducted, where people's apartments were entered without any sort of a court order. As for this authorisation, it stems from the old Law on Criminal Procedure. This authorisation was given to members of certain services, including the public and State Security Service, and they were entitled to use it under certain circumstances. I had a similar authorisation during the 20 years of service, so throughout that time I was entitled to do that. I worked for 25 years in the State Security Service, and I never used this authorisation to enter a premises without a court order and search them. I'm just saying this to illustrate how lightly members of the special detachment within the CSB treated this authorisation. Of course, it was quite easy to pull out your ID, enter somebody's apartment who was fighting for his very life, trying to save his family, and nobody really cared whether what they were doing was lawful, unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what were the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know if you're finished with this, but I have a question of the witness. I see that the phrase is -- appears twice on the back of the card "provided for by law." And if I understand the witness's answer to your last question -- the counsel's last question, it was that this was the old law. And my question is whether this quote/unquote "old law" had ever been repealed or whether it was still in force? Do you understand my question, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. That's my profession; that's from my professional field. We did not change the Law on Criminal Procedure once the war broke out and once Republika Srpska was established. Rather, in 1993, at one of the Assembly sessions of Republika Srpska, we adopted the decision declaring that the Law on Criminal Procedure of the former SFRY was still in force. So it was a uniform law that was in place. We simply adopted a decision extending its validity. And it wasn't until sometime in 2000 that the Law on Criminal Procedure was changed, and those were initially mostly cosmetic changes. And sometime later there were also some substantive changes in order to harmonise that Law on Criminal Procedure with some crimes and in order to have it encompass the situation as it existed before the conflict. I hope I was clear. I think that all of this was done in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Olmsted, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to go back to these searches of apartments that the special police detachment were conducting in 1992, when they conducted these searches, did they take anything from the apartments? And if so, what did they take?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever they considered to be valuable and that they could profit from. So it wasn't just valuables, jewellery, cars, paintings and so on, but everything else; TV sets, VCRs, whatever they could get, even bed linen. Let me just give you an illustration. In the territory of Teslic, they expropriated 147 cars that had a value above average in a month's time, so that was just one example, not to mention other goods worth millions. They looted whatever they could; shops, warehouses. It was really something they took advantage of. Some people who had nothing just before that became wealthy overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to move to another topic now. Did you know about a red kombi --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm a bit confused, because I think that a leading question preceded this answer. When the witness spoke about searches, he spoke about searches in general, not just searches conducted by the special unit, especially when it comes to Teslic and all of these instances of lootings and so on. I had to explain, because this question and this answer put together don't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think that's a matter for cross-examination. I think the witness perfectly understood the question, and it was directed particularly at the special police detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was going to suggest the same thing. Mr. Krgovic, to the extent that you have a concern, it's a note that you would make for when you cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, did you know about a red "kombi" group operating in Banja Luka the beginning of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that every resident of Banja Luka knew of that. The red kombi or red van was actually a hearse, in translation. This was the most awful thing that happened in Banja Luka, a civilised town. Whenever people saw this red van, they would start running away. And whoever had this red van stopped in front of their house could officially announce a period of mourning. These were the people who acted with ill intentions in relation to everybody. People were beaten, harassed. All kinds of things were done by this group which was recognisable because of this red van. I regret that the colour was red. It is my colour. I wish it were of another colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Who were the members of this red kombi group targeting?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while -- or, rather, initially, mostly affluent, respected citizens of Bosniak ethnicity. And later on, when they stole everything they could from them and deported them or did graver things, then it was the turn of those who were Serbs and who in any way opposed their activities. I know of cases where they mistreated Serbs, stole from Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How long did this group operate in Banja Luka for?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a long time. I think that the methodology of work of that group was consistent with the methodology of work of the Chetniks. They operated in "trojkas," in groups of three, and they spread fear among people. They intimidated them so that people would make a decision quicker and easier to leave Banja Luka or so that people would withdraw from public spaces or streets whenever they saw the red kombi so as there would be no witnesses to what they did. Your Honours, by your leave, just one more sentence, just one sentence. I know that what I'm saying is something that can cause grave consequences to me because members of the red kombi group walk freely in Banja Luka nowadays, but I am not uncomfortable speaking about this because these people do not really belong to my nation. They -- this is a deviant behaviour, and they were never called to responsibility for what they had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was this red kombi group functioning throughout 1992, from April through to the end of December 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were active, as far as I remember, throughout 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, Who were the members of this group?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember all of them. I do remember one or maybe two of them. One was called Predrag Boziroda. Boziroda.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. Were there police officers in this group?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were the other members also police officers?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, none of the people who were in this red kombi group were people who were outside of the police force, with one limitation. There is a possibility that some of them or one of them may have had an ID by the SNB, the National Security Service, because the times were difficult and it could happen that some people would have IDs of the State Security Service without even knowing what this service was. They somehow got it from somebody else. There is a possibility, yes, but mostly they were linked up or linked to the CSB in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And from where did this group operate from? What was their headquarters or their base?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the building -- or, rather, let me put it like this: In the -- on the premises that belonged to the CSB, that's where they were located, in the official -- in the official premises, and then they would launch into their actions from the premises that belonged to the CSB. I don't know whether they always took off from the same place or did they use various locations that were part of the CSB. I don't know anything about that. My guess is that it wasn't so. This was simply a criminal group that did what they did for personal gain, and only for personal gain. They were trying to instill fear among the citizens, primarily those of non-Serb ethnicity, yet such activities of theirs were not condoned by the Serbs either. Everyone was afraid of them. One wouldn't dare mention a red kombi or red van in Banja Luka. I don't know whether you can understand that, whether you can understand the feeling. It's just as if somebody would come to a doctor saying, I'm feeling that I have a cold, and then he hears, Oh, no, you actually have cancer, you have about 24 more hours to live. That kind of feeling.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you have any discussions about this red kombi group with Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I can tell you why. Because I talked about the issue with my colleague, Zivko Bojic, with Mr. Vlado Tutus. I also talked about it with people from the military security service. And I remember that Mr. Zivko Bojic told me about Stojan Zupljanin being informed about it and even told me that some kind of arrangement was made to neutralise such groups, including the red van, red kombi. I don't know what was done about it. I am not aware of any specific measures being taken about this group of people. That's all I know about the red van. They committed all sorts of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Mr. Radulovic, I know we're going into a lot of detail about events there that occurred a long time ago, and we're doing it in a limited amount of time. Would it assist you to answer the question I asked you if you took a look at your written statement briefly, and particularly paragraph 95?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I object. I strongly, vigorously object to that. Ask a direct question, not to use the statement. Your Honour, the position of the Defence is this statement is a compilation and consists of only the Prosecution case against the accused, not the real statement. That's the reason we object to tender this as evidence like the 92 ter statement, so that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not asking him to read out loud anything from his prior statement. I'm just seeking clarification because what he's saying -- there is some inconsistency, and I want to just clarify that. If he reads it and that's all he wants to say about it, that's fine. I'm not going to put in the record his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What Mr. -- I appreciate the practical difficulty that you have, Mr. Olmsted, but, as always, counsel must take its witness as he find him. And Mr. Krgovic is more than technically correct. So ask the question and see what answer you elicit. And the witness, himself, was not asked -- it's unusual, let me put it that way, for counsel to invite a witness to refresh his memory from a document, rather than it actually coming from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, but this is -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. This is a written statement that he signed, he reviewed very carefully. It's compiled from his various interviews, so it contains a lot more detail. And since we're asking very specific questions regarding conversations he had with certain individuals, I think it just will assist him if he reviews it, and then I can ask him again the question I wanted to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic has seen the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, they've had it for months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. The problem with the statement is the following: It is a compilation of interviews taken out of the context. And on the occasion of proofing, when we were proofing this witness, he told us that about 30 per cent of it was true and correct and that there were bits missing that need to be elaborated, and this is what he's doing now. He's now elaborating on some of the issues, and this is why I opposed -- and this is why we opposed for the statement to be entered into the evidence. And so we asked for him to testify based on his memories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There is no application for it to be entered into evidence, and I propose, as a practical solution, inasmuch as the statement is available to you and you may make use of it in cross-examination, Mr. Olmsted, you may show him a portion of the statement for him to refresh his memory so that we can move on with this. One of the reasons why I think this should be permitted is I bear in mind that we're dealing with events that would have occurred a long time ago, when the purpose of a trial is not to -- is not a test in memory; it's a question in finding the truth. So if -- Mr. Olmsted, if you could identify the relevant portion. It is not going to be put in evidence, indeed that is not your application, and no doubt Mr. Krgovic would flag it and address it in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just another comment, please. This is a statement from the 12th of -- month of December 2009, so it's not some previous materials that have been compiled. All the discussions, all the interviews, took place in 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: All of those conditions are not lost upon the Trial Chamber, Mr. Krgovic. We appreciate everything that you would have said. And as I indicated earlier, technically speaking, you're correct. Indeed, it is so obvious you probably don't have to argue it. But, as I said, to try to arrive at a practical way of dealing with the immediate problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, could you please turn to paragraph 95 of your written statement. And it's page --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you please take your time and read that paragraph. It's not very long.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You agree with what's written in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, completely. I stated yesterday, when I spoke about the members of SOS who were -- or the term was translated as "special police detachment," but my first informations were those that I received from Mane Popovic, and my reaction was to go to Mr. Stojan Zupljanin and to tell him -- and tell him that people with such a pedigree, with such a history, with such a record, should not be accepted as members of either public or state security, exactly what you can see in the statement. And then Zupljanin responded, among the men, the men that we discussed at the time, were also the people who were within the red kombi or red van group. Since I knew Mr. -- well, rather not a mister, but Predrag Boziroda, and since I knew about some of his activities in this group, red van, I found it illogical to see such people as members -- as regular members of public or state security. That's what I said yesterday as well. And now, since we have this especially stressed in this part, while I was giving this statement I believe I may have stated that it includes members of the red van group, and that's correct. That's the same thing in a nutshell. So the statement wasn't clear enough. And this is where I agree with the Defence lawyer. It is a compilation. It's a compilation based on several reports I drafted. You can see that in the footnote as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And when you brought to Mr. Zupljanin's attention the activities of the SOS as well as the members of the red kombi group, what was his response?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just told you now. Radule, he told me, these are Serbian heroes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Between the 1st of April and 31st of December, 1992, where was your office located?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, before you go to another topic, do we have a Milos report on the red kombi group?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The Prosecution's not in possession of one, but I can ask Mr. Radulovic if he ever wrote one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, did you ever write a report on the activities of the red kombi group?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I remember well a comment I wrote in this report or a comment that Mr. Nedeljko Kesic put in this report of mine saying that this is something we shouldn't be dealing with; in other words, we shouldn't be dealing with gathering information relating to criminal activities by members of CSB, members of this group, the red van group. I remember this well. I believe it may be part of the materials that you have. I managed to find it among the documents that were handed over to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Does that answer your question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Before I move on to the next topic, maybe we should take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We'll return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before the witness comes in, I said to Your Honours after the break I'd give you the numbers, and I said to Mr. Dygeus that I'll give him the sheet of paper afterwards. The documents referred to by Mr. Traynor were as follows: 65 ter 10358.03, 65 ter 3379, 65 ter 3378, 65 ter 3375, 65 ter 10358.07, and 65 ter 3373. Those are the six articles. Your Honours, while I'm on my feet, can I just also mention that next week Mr. Riedlmayer, the expert, if he's an expert, to do with religious destruction is being called; we haven't yet had a ruling from Your Honours on that, so if you would consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, before you continue, you would have been alerted by the Court Officer, whom I thank, because, as I told her, she would -- by speaking with you directly she would identify the problem better than I would be able to at this point, that in terms of the earlier question, the interpreters may not have -- what we would have gotten would not have been what the witness intended to convey, and you've been invited to ask the question again for the record. And I assume it's been -- it's 21 -- the answer appears at page 29, line 3. I believe you have that information, Mr. Olmsted. So before you continue, perhaps you could deal with that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And before I do, I was notified that the document we showed the witness when we were -- testifying about Doboj, P1337, that was only marked for identification previously in this trial, and so we would move to admit it, now that he identified it. It is the document pertaining -- it is the document I showed him pertaining to Doboj and the activities of the special police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's now -- we lift the MFI status, and it's a full exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. Is that the document dated 17th of May? Thank you very much. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, before we took the break, you were looking at paragraph 95 of your written statement. And perhaps you could just turn back to that. There was an issue with regard to the translation of what you testified about that paragraph, and so I'm going to ask my question again. And if you could just briefly repeat again what you told us. And my question was: After you've read this paragraph, does that refresh your recollection with regard to a conversation that you had with Mr. Zupljanin about the red kombi group?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your permission, I said that after having heard that, among others, members of and individuals from this group will be received into the active duties of the service, and I've heard about that from Mane, that these people will be allowed to enter this group. And I went to Stojan Zupljanin and told him that I believed they shouldn't be allowed to become members of active service because their history is not the kind of history that an employee of the public or state security should look like, and I also said what the reaction was of Mr. Zupljanin. What I'd like to stress is that during that conversation - it was a conversation; it wasn't a written communication - that I told him what they had done before, what crimes they've committed. I'm not sure -- what is it that you're asking me to do? I can now elaborate and talk about all of these actions that they were responsible for, but this had to do with my relationship and my contacts with Stojan Zupljanin, which also included discussions about the red kombi group. And could you please correct name "Bodiroga." It turns out I said "Bodiroga," but it's Predrag "Boziroda."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'll just repeat that the only reason we're asking you this question again is because there may have been a mistake in the translation, the English translation, so we apologise for having asked the question again. Just one further confirmation. Will you confirm that Zupljanin's response to you was, Well, Dule, these are Serb heroes?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I can confirm that. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, and I think that clarifies the record. I want to move on to another topic. Between 1 April and 31 December 1992, where was your office located physically?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was located on the premises of the CSB in Banja Luka, in the so-called central building, fourth floor. I think the number of my office was 49, or maybe 149, one of the two. But it was on the fourth floor, and that was the top floor of the building. There is no fifth floor. Milos Group had three offices. I was sitting alone in one of the offices, and then the remaining colleagues were seated two per office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During this time-period, were you aware whether non-Serbs were brought to the CSB building and interrogated?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen very little of it with my own eyes. I've heard of some of these events, but mainly because I spent very little time in Banja Luka. The activities of the Milos Group was almost invariably in the areas outside of Banja Luka. We would come to Banja Luka either late in the day or occasionally we would be away from Banja Luka for several days. And realistically speaking, I did not focus nor did I focus my colleagues to monitor what's going on in the CSB centre because I believed there were others who would be able to notice, observe, possible illegal activities or actions that do not confirm with police work, regular police work. But I did see on occasions that people were brought in and mistreated, and I can give you specific examples. But I do not know who was in charge of interrogation of these people and who was in charge of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. But I think one of the problems here is that you have to understand that when you answer a question, I have to listen to the interpretation, and there is a delay. Just because there's a delay doesn't mean that I just want you to continue with your answer. Just wait after you've answered the question and let me ask another question. But you did mention that you observed some illegal activities during the interrogations of non-Serbs at the CSB building. Could you please provide us what you observed?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I observed that people I knew from the town were being brought to the central building of the CSB, handcuffed, obviously beaten. I could not connect these people with any possible illegal activities, and it in a way all seemed rather surprising to me. Also, some members of Bosniak and Croat people came to my offices in Banja Luka, when I was there, complaining about certain events, certain trends, harassments. They even pointed out to issues related to the disappearance of their nearest and dearest, people who were taken in custody by the so-called members of public or security services. I can't remember his name now, but the owner of the first shopping mall in Banja Luka came to me to tell me that some of our employees took into custody his wife and his mother-in-law. I got interested in the issue, tried to resolve the situation. However, neither the wife nor the mother-in-law were ever found. They're still missing. Therefore, there are grounds to believe that they were killed exclusively because of the huge wealth the family had prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What were the ethnicity of the wife and the mother-in-law?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you had the opportunity to observe these non-Serbs being brought to the CSB building, can you tell us, do you recall who was actually bringing them in on those occasions that you actually observed?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot give you specific names, but these were mainly people who joined the service later, at a later stage. When I say "service," I mean either public or state security, people of whom I do not know that they were members of the special police detachment -- or, rather, I really -- I actually do know that they were a member of the detachment, but I don't know what their names are. I was an employee of the State Security Service. I know the structure well and the individuals -- the staffs of both public and -- of the State Security Service, but the public security service people, I knew only those that I was familiar with privately. Professionally speaking, I knew very little about the staff of the public security service. I knew quite a few of -- a very small number of them by the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, What happened to these non-Serbs during their interrogation at the CSB building?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot, because I didn't take part in those interrogations, especially not during that period. But I know that in 1993 I had an argument with the chief, Nedeljko Kesic, because some Bosniaks had been brought in and mistreated by their interrogators. Predrag Ceranic was in charge of that, who was his then-deputy. People were literally beaten up, and everything -- all their property had been looted. The members that I have mentioned here took part in that activity. They were under the command and under the authority of Ljuban Ecim and Zdravko Samardzija. This went on for a couple of days. I said that it was unnecessary because I had had information about those people from 1990 or 1991. They were members of the SDA, which was a legal political party, the Party of Democratic Action, and they were collected for days and mistreated and beaten because allegedly the service had security-relevant information about their hostile activities. I know that because I spoke to Predrag Ceranic and Nedeljko Kesic on several occasions about that, and I insisted that these people should not be mistreated. In 1992, I know that our former employees of the SJB were also brought in for interrogation. I can relate what they went through, what kind of mistreatment, but I didn't witness that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: These former colleagues from the SJB, were they non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And focusing on 1992, in 1992 what information did you have about any mistreatment of these former colleagues of yours or any other none Serbs at the CSB building?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that I wasn't much involved, but I know of a case when one of the former chiefs of the security service - he was either chief or deputy chief - he had to unload coal for the CSB, which didn't make sense because only recently the man was a colleague, an active serviceman. I saw that as a humiliation for him. I think that his name was Ibrabegovic [phoen] or something, I'm not sure, but something similar. We pointed that out, too, because I saw that as something that I had already observed in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that example. This information you received about the mistreatment of non-Serbs at the CSB building, did you communicate that to Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Kesic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Mr. Kesic, yes. And I said that my contacts with Mr. Stojan Zupljanin were rare and only under certain circumstances, when it was really required. Otherwise, I was not in contact with Mr. Zupljanin; certainly not daily, maybe not even weekly. I forwarded such information through Bera [Realtime transcript read in error "Beara"] to Mr. Kesic, but I related much information to Mr. Kesic directly about these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This mistreatment of non-Serbs at the CSB building, was it done --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Just 38, 1, I believe the witness said "Bera," not "Beara." It might be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's "Bera."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This mistreatment of non-Serbs at the CSB building in 1992, was its frequency and where it occurred open enough that it could be observed by pretty much anyone, or was this something done very secretly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's calling for speculation. If you look at the previous witness, he wasn't there most of that time, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, he did observe a few instances himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say how frequent, exactly, that was and who was in a position to see that. I know from experience that I observed some things and my colleagues didn't, although I had been there only for 15 minutes and they had been there for 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you ever visit Manjaca Camp in 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us approximately when that was, what month?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1992. It could have been in July or August. I know that it was summertime, and I know why I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what did you observe about the conditions at the camp?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, briefly, it was horrible. There were no conditions for biological survival, no hygiene at all. The food was extremely bad. There was a huge number of people on a very small -- in a very small space. Most of them had gone through physical mistreatment. What else should I say? There was a group there that would physically mistreat every prisoner when they were brought there, and many prisoners died in Manjaca of the consequences of these beatings. When I say "many," I must say that even two or three is many, to my mind, but certainly a much greater number must have died for these reasons. And many were maimed. I don't want to go into the mental consequences, but the physical consequences certainly were grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that they were prisoners. Was this an open camp or was it a detention facility?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a detention facility. And when I say that, I mean any facility with a fence around it and guards and from which nobody can leave without permission or an order of the ones guarding them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This information that you observed or learned about Manjaca Camp and the treatment of the detainees there, did you provide this information to Mr. Kesic and Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did inform Mr. Kesic, and he said that this wasn't our concern, that it was under the authority of the VRS. Frankly speaking, he told me not to meddle. That's roughly it. But it wasn't only once. We spoke about it on several occasions. Unfortunately, he didn't accept any of my suggestions. He never granted any of my requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you also speak to Mr. Zupljanin about Manjaca Camp?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having spoken to Zupljanin about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps to refresh your recollection, you could look at paragraph 170 of your written statement and just read it to yourself and see if that refreshes your recollection. If it doesn't, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a cross-examination. If this is how it is supposed to continue, showing the witness a statement every now and then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: How many times -- the ruling that I gave earlier was, I thought, exceptional. How many times is this exercise going to be pursued?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps could we talk about this without the witness listening in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, could you please remove your headphones. Mr. Olmsted, my concern is that we're dealing with a question of the proper application of the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is, of course -- this testimony is not a memory test. He's testifying about a whole bunch of events that occurred in 1992. We've only even touched on some of them. And obviously we have limited time, and we're trying to get out the evidence at quickly as possible. We're not asserting that the witness is being untruthful. I think he's trying to give the truth. But because of -- this so much information, in addition because he is here as a Serb testifying against Serbs, and he's also here with his boss -- his former boss, it's a difficult situation for him, and we just want the truth to come out and have him an opportunity to refresh his memory with regard to the certain things he says in his statement, not bringing that statement into the record at all. And this is merely to speed up the process, so I'm not asking him tons of questions about these issues. I don't know -- I can't say how often I'll have to use it, but I'm trying to use it only in particular instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: When I asked how often you would have to use it, that was really a rhetorical question. The thing is the Chamber has ruled on the use of these statements as matters which may be exhibited, and we are -- it would be inconsistent with what we would have previously ruled to allow you to go down the path which you seem now intent on pursuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would have thought that one of the skills of counsel is being faced with, as I said earlier, you take your witness as you find him, to phrase your questions in order to get the information that you seek. The Chamber has ruled on the broad question of the admissibility of these statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And certainly under the guide-lines, Your Honour, you have the power to determine the means and circumstances in which a witness's memory can be refreshed. Here he says he doesn't recall something, and I can't speak for every jurisdiction, but the jurisdiction I come from, you certainly can refresh a witness's memory from his prior statements or basically anything, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I was about to say I'm not sure the Rules are that wide, but the rules with which I'm familiar is that one of the conditions precedent for a witness to refresh his memory is that the document must be virtually contemporaneous. And one of the deficiencies - for want of a better word - in this case is that -- and this was at the heart of Mr. Krgovic's earlier observation, is that we're dealing with a recent compilation. So, in other words, there's a remoteness to the events with which -- about which a witness is testifying and the refreshing-memory document, which is a cause of concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're correct that the statement was made not in -- back in 1992, but it was made in conditions where it was extensive interviewing going on. He had the opportunity to review a large number of documents and really think and spend time reflecting on these events, and the situation, of course, is very much different in the courtroom, where he is subject to pressure, nervousness of testifying here, the fact that he's testifying in open session. Some of the things he says are quite powerful. And so in those circumstances all we're seeking to do is to refresh his memory regarding a prior statement he made. I don't want to ask leading questions, and that's what I'm trying to avoid. And by refreshing his memory, then asking my question again, which is not leading, it's perhaps going to speed up the whole process. And that's really all we're trying to achieve here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, efficiency is merely one aspect. Another overriding aspect of our trial is conduct and fairness, is more important. May we have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Again, we take a practical approach to this. And as with the last -- the last time this arose, the witness may read the relevant portion of his statement, and then you may ask your question, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, I apologise for that. We just had to argue a very procedural matter, and now we can get back on to our topic. If you could please take a look at paragraph 170, and if you could just read that short paragraph completely to yourself.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And my question to you is: Does that refresh your recollection regarding a conversation you had with Stojan Zupljanin about Manjaca Camp?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing special. I can only repeat that in 1992 there had been too many conversations, especially between me and Kesic. Well, I also spoke about many events to Mr. Stojan Zupljanin too, but I'm not sure that I orally informed Mr. Zupljanin of the conditions at Manjaca. I don't remember. Although I saw what I stated and what I signed, but part of the statement refers to my report number 238. And if that is contained in my report, then that is much more credible than what I may or may not remember after such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss with Mr. Zupljanin under whose jurisdiction Manjaca Camp fell?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let me tell you, when I wrote that report about Manjaca and when I informed Kesic of the events there, I know that Kesic said to me then that it was not our concern, that I shouldn't meddle, that it's under the authority of the army; simply speaking, that we should steer clear of it. I considered it the duty of our service to inform of such things because I considered our service the most important link between politics and the situation on the ground, some sort of connecting tissue. I was at Manjaca, but I was also at Gradiska and Omarska, and I considered all that intolerable. That cannot be in the interests of the Serbian people, and it cannot be the objective of the Serbian people to keep persons in such camps who are innocent, who were simply taken there because they have names of a certain type or because they belonged to a certain religious or ethnic group. I didn't write that because it was my wish to go outside of the scope of the interests of the service. It was my opinion that the service had to register such things and inform those above us, inform the politicians. And being here, I can add we noticed that information about these things wasn't being passed on, so we tried to get this information to the political leadership through military security. There was a man in military security at the time, and later he would become the leader of the Typhoons. We tried to forward such information through him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radulovic. And, again, I just have to keep on reminding you - I apologise for this - but please try to keep your answers short. You mentioned Mr. Kesic and you were reporting this information regarding Manjaca Camp as well as other matters affecting public security --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: May I just intervene for a moment. The witness referred to one of his reports, and if it's correct in the transcript, it would be report number 238. Can we establish a link with one of the reports on your list? Is it or isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, we don't have all his reports, and it's not on our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's not on your list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We don't have that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: As I was saying, you were reporting this information regarding Manjaca Camp and, in fact, other matters affecting public security to Mr. Kesic. Did he have an obligation to report those matters then on to Stojan Zupljanin as well as to the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at P411.18. I'll just make sure that I said it right. It's P411.18. Yes, this is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, is this one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's mine, or, rather, a report of my group.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It states that the TO, Serbian police, and volunteers took all key installations in Sanski Most, and almost all extreme members of the SDA fled the municipality. When you wrote "Serbian police," who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean those who fled, they were the leaders of the SDA party, reputable Bosniaks from the area, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, but let me re-ask my question. You write in here that the "Serbian police," among others, "took all key installations in Sanski Most." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
