utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, and it's true. I don't know what there is to comment. It is true. The Serb forces took all significant facilities at Sanski Most and established, well, let's call it Serb rule in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the only thing I'm seeking clarification at this point is: You say "Serbian police," and that's a general term. And could you be more specific as to who you mean by "Serbian police"? Was it the SJB members? Was it the CSB? Who were the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say "Serbian police," meaning police from Serbia, no. I meant active and reserve policemen from the Sanski Most Police Station, TO members, and various volunteers who appeared grouped in various groups, unlike specialists who called themselves some sort of Chetniks. So it was a complex situation. Whoever had weapons belonged to a group that they thought they should belong to, except for organised forces that belonged to the Territorial Defence, Serbian police. It was a mixed-up situation in Sanski Most. There were different kinds of mistreatments on various grounds, so whoever was in the position to leave Sanski Most safely and were of a different ethnicity, that is to say, they were Croats or Bosniaks, did so because they were scared, they didn't want to test their luck, and they left. Those who remained were those who were not able to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned volunteers, and this document we're looking at also mentions volunteers. Could you tell us whether that -- you're referring to the SOS or S-O-S in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, according to your intelligence information, was there any organised armed resistance in Sanski Most by the non-Serb population either during this take-over or following it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no information about any specifically-organised resistance movement, but there were instances of Croats and Bosniaks in that area attempting to organise themselves and organising some sorts of groups and so on. It wasn't typical for Sanski Most. It was more typical for other areas such as Prijedor, Kljuc, and some other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So in your assessment, did the non-Serbs who remained in Sanski Most - and you've just mentioned these were non-Serbs who really didn't have the means to leave the municipality - did they pose any threat to Serb control over that municipality?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything specifically about that. I did not make any assessments or evaluations. But if I were to use my work experience and the information I had coming from that area, I don't think that they were a significant safety and security risk for the Serbian authorities in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 2D21.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you confirm whether this is one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, this report is -- the previous report we looked at was dated 24 April 1992. This particular report that we're looking at right now is dated 7 March 1992, and it does mention that Muslims in Sanski Most owned a few thousand long-barrelled rifles. Can you tell us what happened between early March and the time of the take-over in the middle of April that prevented the non-Serbs from mounting a significant armed resistance against the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain. Before the take-over of power, almost all members of Bosniak units had withdrawn to the Bihac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we please take a look at 65 ter 2840.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Mr. Radulovic, can you confirm whether this is one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Unless Your Honours have any questions regarding this document, I'm just going to seek to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1374, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we please look at P693. And if we could turn just quickly to the page number 2 of this document. Oh, actually, no, leave it there. Leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see at the top it says "Radulovic, Sajinovic, Stjepanovic," and it's dated 16 October 1992. Sir, is this one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could take a look at the second page of the B/C/S. I think it's the bottom of the page of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It states here: "Around 20.000 Muslims have moved out of this region, and the remaining 10.000 or so wish to do the same. Muslims have been moving out of this region mostly because of its uncertain future and lack of security. This uncertainty is due to the wilful behaviour of individuals and groups who abuse citizens of Muslim background and exert pressure on them." To your knowledge, did the Sanski Most SJB take any measures in 1992 to stop this abuse of non-Serb population in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few or insignificant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we take a look at 65 ter 410.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, can you confirm whether this is one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It states that: "In the early-morning hours ... the most important buildings in Prijedor were occupied, and all roads leading to the town were blocked by armed formations of the Serbian people." Can you tell us which armed formations of the Serbian people you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a number of groups established on a voluntary basis, comprising volunteers. I can't call them either parapolice or paramilitary. At the time, we used to denote them as armed formations of the Serbian people. I know that some of them were under the control of the army, some of them were not, not of the police either, and that's what I could tell you in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you have information that the police from the SJB Prijedor participated in the take-over of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I may add, we, as the Milos Group, were concerned. You keep referring to me, personally. All of the reports are a product of collective work of all of us who were members of the Milos Group. What I'm trying to say, that during this period of time in Prijedor we were concerned by the fact that individuals committed various mistreatment and crimes, victimising non-Serbs. We were concerned by such phenomena, as a result of which we informed the SDB and our superiors, believing that together with SJB and together with the military security, they should do something about reintroducing discipline and law and order and put those armed formations under control in order to protect citizens, regardless of what ethnicities they were. I never made distinctions on the basis of what ethnicity they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what response did you receive to that? Did you receive -- were any actions taken to stop these crimes?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after this report, there came a period of a very difficult situation in Prijedor when nobody was safe, least of all Bosniaks and Croats. Briefly - and this is a very long story, but I'll tell you this briefly - it wasn't until a commission came from Banja Luka that the number of crimes significantly decreased, as well as instances of mistreatment of non-Serbs, but it wasn't until much later that this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And are you -- in that last statement that you're referring to, are you talking about the camps in Prijedor, or are you talking about crime in general in Prijedor? Just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to everything, the crimes that were committed not only in Prijedor, but in the wider area of Prijedor municipality, such as Hodzeni [phoen], Brisevo, Hambarine, Kozarac, Trnopolje. I was also referring to what was happening in Omarska, Keraterm, to what was happening within the police station in Prijedor. I simply meant not only the ordinary crimes committed but also what we believed fell into the category of war crimes and crimes against the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This commission, was this in 1992 or is it later in 1993?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this happened in 1992. I remember well; I was in Prijedor for work. I don't know to what extent it is important for all of you here, to give you the reasons for my presence, but, at any rate, that was my first physical presence in Prijedor, and I saw something that I couldn't believe was happening. I visited the camp in Keraterm and the one in Omarska, and I saw something I could not comprehend; the attitude of the guards and of personnel who were guarding the detainees. The conditions were unbearable in a very small space, in closed space. There were too many detainees who were taken out for questioning and brought back all bloody and beaten up, and that was the condition they had been in when taken to questioning. That first experience I had with that caused me to first go to the SDB team, headed by Vojin Bera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We're going to talk about your visit to Omarska and Keraterm in detain in a little bit, but I really want to try to address some preliminary matters before we go to that. So please follow my questions. But just to clarify, I want to get down this commission you've mentioned. This commission, was that after you visited the camps? Is this a commission that was formed to visit the camps? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Can we tender this document into evidence, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can we -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry. Exhibit P1375, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can we take a look at 65 ter 10191.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, what you have before you is a report dated 7 September 1992. Is this one of your -- not your, but your team's Milos reports?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just take a look at the first few sentences, and can you tell us what the purpose of this report was, what were you trying to report?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the report is self-explanatory, but I will tell you that we attempted, by way of this report, to put on notice the leadership of our service, that this is something that the highest political and military echelons in Republika Srpska should be made aware of so that there would be an end to crimes and mistreatment in Prijedor municipality. I have to tell you that the citizens of Serb ethnicity took these crimes in Prijedor with great difficulty. I was present when operatives of the public security turned to me for advice as to what to do; should they leave the service, should they flee Republika Srpska; because they refused to be associated in any way with such kind of work in commissions, investigations team, in public security, military security, and so, due to the attitude that the guards had vis-à-vis detainees who were brought in for questioning. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You indicate in this report that Prijedor buildings are still being unnecessarily destroyed and non-Serbs are forcibly expelled and even killed. Was this the first report you submitted concerning such crimes against the non-Serb population in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: By the time of this report, which is 7 September 1992, was the non-Serb population that was remaining in Prijedor posing any threat to Serb control of that municipality?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before this date and after this date, no. It did not represent a danger either before this date or after this date. After an operation that was conducted in relation to combat activities in Hambarine and Kozarac, following that time, Bosniaks represented no danger whatsoever when it came to military or any other activities in the territory of Prijedor. This operation took place much before this date, the 7th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we will address those attacks on Hambarine and Kozarac in just a minute. But according to your intelligence information, who was committing these crimes against the remaining non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of groups committing crimes, and there were members of police involved in those instances where Croats or Bosniaks were mistreated, both active and reserve policemen of the police station in Prijedor. Simo Drljaca gave his consent directly for such activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You also mention in this report mass graves locations. Which mass graves are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mass graves in Rudnik, Ljubija, and Tomasica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who was buried at these locations, these mass graves?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it was mostly the innocent civilian victims who were buried, of Bosniak and Croat ethnicity, most likely. In Hambarine it was Bosniaks. In Brisevo, mostly Croats. And as for the victims of Donja Ljubija area, it was the Bosniaks. And then the wider area of Kozarac -- you have to understand that 20.000 Bosniaks lived in Kozarac, some Croats, and some belonging to a group called "Others," minorities of Czech or Polish origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer, these mass graves contained non-Serb victims of the attacks on Kozarac, Hambarine, Brisevo, as well as other villages in that area?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you write any reports about these mass graves that provided more detailed information than you provided in this report up your chain of command about these graves?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I gave more detailed reports. And as for the events in Prijedor, if I analyse everything I wrote, I think that my most detailed reports were about the events in Prijedor. I talked more to Kesic and Vojin Bera about these events than about the events in Teslic and Doboj because I believed that the consequences of such behaviour of individuals, including members of the state and public security, were horrendous. In 1992, as I wrote this report, I qualified this, Your Honours, as a case of genocide. And I don't know why now, after 17 or 18 years have passed, I would give a different qualification to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps this is an appropriate time for a break. I'm sorry, can I ask one -- well, I can ask it after the break, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, we have been alerted to your -- for the matter you wish to raise. Would it suffice if we were to release the witness about five minutes -- excuse the witness about five minutes early?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, in early summer of 1992, was there an attack by Serb forces on the village of Brisevo? I think you've already mentioned something about that.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us which Serb forces participated in that attack?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I had information according to which these were members of armed formations who had arrived from the area of Sanski Most. I cannot tell you exactly what the name of the unit or their command was, but these were armed formations from the area of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall, were they VRS forces or were they paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And according to your intelligence information, was there any armed resistance by the Croat population in Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us what happened to the civilian population in Brisevo during the attack?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They suffered as victims. There were even casualties among children below the age of seven. I couldn't give you a number of the victims, but, in any case, a very large number of victims for a village in a very small area, in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: After the attack, what remained of the village?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think anything remained there; only traces of what was burned, destroyed. And victims, the bodies, were removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to actually visit Brisevo sometime after the attack and witness what the village looked like, yourself?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not directly, not in the village itself, but I did have an opportunity to see the village from a vantage point. I spent a lot of time in the area of Ljubija, Gornja Ljubija, Prijedor, Brisevo, Niska Rijeka. My wife hails from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This information about what happened to the non-Serb population during the attack on Brisevo, where did you obtain this intelligence information?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily from employees of the public security service who were working from the station department of the Ljubija Police Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Around this same time-period as the Brisevo attack, was there also an attack by Serb forces on the village of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the village of Hambarine, it took place a bit earlier. The conditions were different. The Hambarine village, there was a group of Bosniaks who had military organisation, were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us which Serb forces participated in the attack of that village?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot -- I'm not familiar with insignia on uniforms, but there were volunteers, members of the police special detachment, together with the police from Prijedor, reserve police from Prijedor. At the time of the operations in the area of Hambarine, I was present there for a shorter period, for one day, so I even was an eye-witness to some of these combat operations. And I would like to ask -- when I'm saying "me, personally," I still refer to the whole group, the Milos Group. Very seldom I went out without the entire group being together.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned in your last answer the special police. Was that the special police of the CSB Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Since you were there, where was the detachment positioned during the attack?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that, but I encountered some of the special detachment members - we were passing each other - because between me -- or, rather, the Milos Group and the members of the special detachment, there was certain tension, one could feel it between us, and it was possible at any point that there would be an armed conflict, even, between us. And since they were stronger, our assessment was to try to and avoid such contacts because they might lead to direct armed conflicts. We were, in comparison to them, humane human beings; whereas they would stop at nothing. They didn't have any dignity. And we had to bear in mind that it wouldn't necessarily only be us but also our families who they could target. There were some threats issued as well. You can imagine what kind of situation it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What triggered the attack on Hambarine? Was there a particular event that triggered it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To put it as short as possible, on an occasion some members of the Territorial Defence came to a check-point which was set up by the Bosniaks from Hambarine. I think one was killed of the Territorial Defence members and one was seriously wounded. And that started this series of armed conflicts. And then that, furthermore, led to the eruption of this cleansing or mopping-up of terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... members of TO was killed and one was wounded. In transcript, it says one was killed, one was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that that's not what he said?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, in your last answer, at the check-point, did you say that it was one TO member who was killed and one who was seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember the events, and as far as I remember what I've just said, there were two killed and one was seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the Bosniak population in Hambarine able to offer any meaningful resistance to this attack?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an evaluation of that. I had information that they are organised in a way, in a military manner, but I didn't have specific, exact information about how many armed men are there, what kind of armaments they have, what kind of logistics; as opposed to the situation in Kozarac about which I had much more detailed information and more reliable. So I cannot give you an opinion about whether they believed they actually could put up some kind of more meaningful resistance. I guess they would have known best about these things. But I do believe it would have been illogical for them to start all that, because Ljubija, Gornja, was behind them, which was under the control of the Serbian forces; Prijedor was under Serbian authority; so they only had one way out of the encirclement, and that is towards Kozarac. So if they had a reasonable commander, I'd say he would not allow them to initiate any kind of armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: After the attack on Hambarine, what remained of the village? Was it seriously damaged?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And if I may say, we had a repetition of what we've seen before; namely, whatever wasn't destroyed during the armed conflict itself would be destroyed immediately after the operations. After the searches had been conducted, after everything had been stolen, everything would be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what happened to the civilian population in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the civilians got killed, and some were expelled or maybe driven away from the area, if you prefer it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's move to Kozarac. Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, can I ask, Did the witness write a report on Hambarine? And if so, do we have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll answer the second question first. We don't have reports on the crimes that were committed in Hambarine or Brisevo, I don't believe. Otherwise, we'd be showing it to the witness. But I'll ask him the first part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, we've talked about Brisevo and Hambarine so far, and we're going to talk about Kozarac next. Did you write reports on what you learned about what happened to the civilian populations in these villages in 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for a fact that we did write reports because our practice was to put into writing whatever information we gathered. So the fact that we haven't -- that you haven't found these reports, well, I don't know anything about that. But the vault that I had or the strong box that I had in my office, and that remained in Banja Luka, there was 2.750 pages of documentation. You presented to me only about 1200 pages, which means that about 1250 pages are missing that were drafted by the Milos Group, and that more than half of the reports submitted by us is missing. You must understand that I did not keep my private archives where all these documents would be stored, but I know for a fact that we reported about events in Hambarine, in Ljubija, in Kozarac. I have seen some of the documents. They were shown to me by you. You can put questions about those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radulovic. Mr. Olmsted, could you, at any convenient moment, check whether document 10190 could concern Hambarine, not necessarily now at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it does, but it's not on our exhibit list, and that's why I didn't show him -- it's about the check-point incident, and I figured that he got that -- we got that out sufficiently without the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's talk about Kozarac. Now, what Serb forces participated in the attack of that village?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same: members of the VRS, active, reserve, and conscript elements; then police, active and reserve; paramilitary formations. I do not have information concerning participation of the police special detachment from the CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think we have already evidence that the attack on Kozarac was essentially around the same time as the attack on Hambarine. Is it fair to say that the attack on Kozarac was triggered by the same event as the attack on Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A casualty was an active captain of the VRS, as well as one soldier, and I think that one soldier was seriously wounded. Exactly the same kind of incident; barricades, there was shooting. But that route -- that road used to be blocked for a period of time, the road between Banja Luka and Prijedor, which was a serious problem because a big part of the territory was cut off. One had to travel using roundabout ways, bad roads between Prijedor and Banja Luka and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. A part of the answer was not recorded. I believe the witness mentioned that there was a barricade there. Maybe you can clarify that with the witness, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you -- Mr. Radulovic, in your last answer did you refer to a barricade?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did refer to a barricade. It was on the road from Banja Luka to Prijedor, and there was another one on the way back. So on the entrances to the village, there were barricades with armed people, members of Bosniak ethnicity in the area. And not only in that area, in the wider area of Kozarac they set up a defence circle with armed formations guarding the entrances into the village against the Serbian policemen and Serbian forces. It was organised -- well organised. They had squads, companies, and so on; namely, establishment strength was a brigade strength. They had primarily infantry arms but also some artillery pieces. These were called Charlies. I don't know how many pieces they had. I also don't know how many other artillery pieces they had, but I do know that they were rather well armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. But, again, my question was just about the barricades, and you provided much more information. And I appreciate your efforts to provide as much information as possible, but please just focus on the question again. What happened to the civilian Bosniak population after this attack on Kozarac? What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost all of them ended up in collection centres such as Trnopolje or in camps such as Keraterm and Omarska. Why am I making this distinction between a collection centre and a camp? Let me explain. Trnopolje was a place where they treated people less harsh than in Keraterm or Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'll ask the same question as I asked about the other villages. What was left of the Bosniak houses and mosques and other premises in the village of Kozarac after the attack?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost nothing remained. There used to be five mosques there, and all five of them were destroyed. There is seven mosques there, newly built, and the village was completely reconstructed, except for something that is, of course, most difficult to reconstruct; namely, there aren't many of the people who used to live there before the war. Many of them met tragic death. A lot of people know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 433.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you confirm this is one of your team's reports?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it's dated 28 May 1992, and it states that during the attack on Kozarac the Serb forces lost, it reports, only five men, while the non-Serbs lost several hundred. Was that, in fact, the case?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's stated in our report. We had such information at the time. Whether anything changed at least in relation to casualties on the Serb side or whether any other changes, this is the information we had at least in May, and what's in it is what we knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The report also states that a huge number of persons have been arrested and some have surrendered, and it talks about problems providing them shelter or a place to be, and includes women, children, and old people. Are these people people that ended up in the camps that you just told us about a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them ended up in the so-called Collection Centre Trnopolje, and those who were of better health or those who were able-bodied men who could be members of the army, who looked more fit, they were imprisoned in Keraterm and Omarska. I don't know whether you're familiar with that. This Omarska location and the very location where these people were incarcerated was a location that belonged to the Ljubija Mine. The building there where they were housed belonged to the Ljubija Mine complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, obviously you were horrified about this information you received about the crimes committed in these villages during the attacks. Do you recall that you discussed this information with Mr. Zupljanin two or three months later?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discussed the events in Prijedor with Mr. Zupljanin. On how many occasions, I don't know, but I can tell you that we had quite a few discussions in relation to the events in Prijedor. I even remember that we proposed for Simo Drljaca to be removed in one way or the other. We assessed that he was crazy, that he was a maniac. I can say whatever I want about him because he's dead now, but I can say that I pulled out my Hekler pistol and pointed at him, put it in his mouth, actually wanting to kill him after I've seen what had been done there, and it was just my humanity that prevented me from doing that. He didn't know who I was, so he was startled by it all, and I didn't know who he was. So this vicious circle was broken only when the commander of the police station, Dusan Jankovic, showed up, who in 1984 was a member of my team when we provided security for the Olympic Games, who told me that I must quickly get out of Prijedor because Simo Drljaca would not forgive and forget and he would kill me as well as all the members of my group.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we tender this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1376, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, can I put one question to the witness. About the statement that on the Serb side there was a loss of five men, and ten having been wounded, whereas it is estimated that enemy losses amount to several hundred men, speaking of enemy losses, does this refer to armed men, or is it a total number of casualties within the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we were talking about total numbers, referring to total numbers. We didn't have even an opportunity to try and determine which of the casualties were members of armed formations and which civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 1151. This is a report dated 30 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you confirm whether this is a report by your team?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It states there is a lack of professionalism on the part of the Prijedor SJB and TO commanding personnel and states that the problem of detained and captured persons of Muslim background is still present. What do you mean by "lack of professionalism" on the part of the Prijedor SJB leadership?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, when you have such total confusion, lack of organisation; when there's not proper accommodation available to people who were taken into custody for some reason or another; when one doesn't know what the interrogations are about; when there were -- when there are no preceding operational activities aimed at determining whether a person was a member of enemy formations, of Green Berets; when the teams aren't organised in a way to have members who know how to deal with issues professionally and fairly. And I also believe that simply their approach was not professional, not competent, with the exception of some employees either of the state or public security services, who did somehow manage to keep up the reputation of, let's say, not only Republika Srpska, but the Serbian people as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Based on your intelligence information that was available to you, were these non-Serbs that were detained by the police of any security interest?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the security interest, I really didn't see any special significance in locking these people up, or I didn't see that this was in our interest. I did observe many elderly people, women, and children in some locations. I will never accept that this may have been the interest of my people. This was, instead, the interest of criminals and crooks or profiteers, people who didn't think that there would be a tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P137 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This document isn't on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's 65 ter 1151.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Was the number given?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1377, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We confirm that it certainly was on our 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, you mentioned a while ago that you visited Omarska and Keraterm camps yourself in 1992, and I want to talk about that. But before we do: Before you visited the camps, had your intelligence team received any information about what was going on at Omarska and Keraterm before you went there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had some information. Our most important goal was to check who, of the collaborators of the SDB, I mean, the pre-war collaborators, and our operational connections, was in those camps. We could not believe that people were kept under such conditions and that such measures were being applied to them. We were especially horrified by the scenes that we saw, and I mean the Milos Group, that in the so-called triages - which -- that's a term they used - active servicemen of the SDB and the SJB took part. And I know many of them as experienced and ethical people, and I couldn't understand why they were there. If they were unable to resist, they could have walked out, escaped. I would never have consented to taking part in what they did. And when I learned that the number-one man behind all these triages, investigations, and so on was Vojin Bera, it became clear to me that anything was possible, because he was a classic sycophant, and this is why the accused, Mr. Zupljanin, never got true information, or at least not before we passed it on to him, before we informed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, this information that you received before you came to Omarska and Keraterm about abuses of the detainees there, did you write reports on that information?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just briefly, I believe that we sent a dispatch to Nedeljko Kesic. And at the time, Vojin Bera was not in Banja Luka so we handed it directly to Kesic, and I believe that it was one of the reasons why we went. I told you what the most important reason was, but we also went there to check what was going on. And, yes, I almost forgot, Mr. Marko Lazovic from the SDB of Serbia called me up and told me that he had some information about something happening in Prijedor and that he suspected that crimes were being committed. And speaking as a colleague, he said to me, Starisa [as interpreted], go there and check there as soon as possible and find out what's really happening. I went there, among others, also to inform the SDB of Serbia because I saw that they were interested. I wrote the report when I came back, which is a longer report. I don't know whether you saw it. And then I was called to come to Belgrade to tell them in more detail what I had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we'll get more into that in a minute. You mentioned that there were these triages at Omarska and Keraterm, and you mentioned that they consisted of someone from the SDB and someone from public security. Who was the third party in this triage?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And military security, please, members of the military security too. I said I was horrified because I had seen members of the state security and public security, but I failed to add that among those who conducted the investigations, there were also people from military security. All these three structures were together and under the direct command, if you will, or acted upon the orders of Vojin Bera. He was charged of these triages, checkups, investigations, and all that for -- he was -- he headed or issued order to all these three teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, the interpreter didn't catch the third security service that was involved, and I think that's important to have on the record. 69, 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Radulovic, but just so the record is clear, can you just very simply tell us who were the three persons involved in these triages, where did they come from, in each of these triages?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't speak about three persons; I spoke about three security services. Those present were members of public security - I believe about a dozen; then there were staff of national security - I believe about 14 of them, with a detachment of national security from Prijedor; and there were also members of military security. In all, there were -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And these triages, did they only function in the camps in Prijedor, or were they in other municipalities in the region?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that the detainees at Keraterm and Omarska - and I'm sure of what I'm saying - had gone through investigative -- the investigative procedure. And if you ask me about other areas, I can tell you that it was just the same in Gradiska. People were called in for interviews. And those people were detainees in those camps. And the situation was the same in other areas also.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What about Sanski Most? Were these triages working in the detention facilities in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I wasn't there personally, I didn't see it with my own eyes, but I was very close with one of the most important people in the SJB in the area of Sanski Most, and I'm still on good terms with him today. He complained to me about the way these interviews were conducted, how these people were being processed, and he told me about the same thing that I told you about the investigations conducted in and around Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now I want to turn to your visit to Omarska and Keraterm camps. Can you tell us how soon after these camps were established that you actually visited them?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. I don't have that information. I think that some 20 days or maybe a month elapsed. I'm a bit lost in time, though, because it's been a long time, but I remember well what I saw with my own eyes at Keraterm and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you visit both those camps the same day?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning hours, I was at Keraterm; and in the afternoon, I was at Omarska. The distance is about 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Since you visited Keraterm Camp first, let's talk about that one first. What did you observe about the conditions for the detainees at that camp? You mentioned that they were crowded, very crowded, but what else did you observe when you visited it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a huge hall. By the way, Keraterm was a factory of ceramic tiles for the construction industry. It was impossible to count the people in that hall. Whether they -- there would have been 800 or a thousand, I really can't tell, but people were crammed together like sardines. They couldn't even sit, let alone lie down. And I know that it was sunny and hot. People couldn't get water. And you couldn't even think of hygiene or sanitation. And individuals were taken from that hall to another building, which was the office building of Keraterm, for interviews, for interrogation, and most everybody who was taken from one building to another was beaten on the way and mistreated physically. The first information about this mistreatment I received from SJB staff, who complained to me that you cannot simply have those who are bringing in the detainees refrain from beating them and mistreating them, so they were -- they were brought in for interviewing bloody, and they returned even bloodier. Although these people belonged to the same people as me, I cannot consider them as such. To me, they are just criminals. I have a universal view of crime and criminals. To me, a criminal is a criminal, irrespective of his ethnicity, whether he is a Serb, Croat, or a Bosniak. To me it's a universal category, which is hostile to me and hostile to my ideology and my people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you see any women, elderly, or children at the camp when you visited that day?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Keraterm, I saw a very small number of females, but I couldn't see much because I was unable to access all parts of the space where they were kept. I watched or looked in through a door, and I saw those standing closest, so I couldn't tell whether at the other end there were women or children, but I did see a certain number of women.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall who you saw guarding the camp when you visited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I'm a little bit confused here. Are we talking about Omarska, or Keraterm, or both?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We're just talking about Keraterm. We'll move to Omarska next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At Keraterm, who was guarding the camp?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood this to be about Keraterm. Whatever I said -- I have said so far is about Keraterm. I can't give you their names, but they were reserve police officers and active-duty police officers. I cannot say that there were no soldiers among them, but I did recognise some public security staff because I could tell by the uniform whether someone was a reserve SJB man or an active-duty SJB man or, alternatively, a military man. At Keraterm, I did not see any members of military units among the guards, all the time referring to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And now let's move to Omarska Camp. After you visited Keraterm, you said that you went to Omarska Camp. When you arrived at Omarska, again, I think you mentioned previously that you observed the conditions were very crowded there for the detainees. What else did you observe about the conditions at that camp when you visited it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw at Keraterm was horrible, but what I saw at Omarska was much more horrible. At the administrative building at Omarska, the administrative building of the mine, I met a lot of my colleagues from the SNB and SJB, and I saw that there were members of the military security there as well whom I didn't know from before. Since I wanted to collect as much information as possible about what was going on at Omarska and Keraterm, I went up to a room which is above the cafeteria, and then from a window there I looked at the back side of that building. There was a yard there covered with grass, and in two or three places I saw silhouettes, people whom I couldn't recognise, and I probably would not have been able to recognise them had I known them from before. So I asked, What is going on? Who made these people lie here in the sun and torture them thus? And then an experienced worker of the SNB told me, using my nickname, Pile, are you pretending to be crazy or are you blind? And since that person used to be my superior, chief of the SNB who retired in the meantime, I asked him, Well, what's the problem? And he said to me, Well, these are dead men. I said, What do you mean, dead men? He said, Well, they were shot from the roof. There is a competition between different armed formations as to where are they going to hit these people, and they bet on beer. So that was the -- that was how much human life was worth there. So me being me, I started cursing, using all the curses that came to my mind. Of course, I didn't see Vojin Bera there, because he mostly was never present where he was supposed to be present and never knew what he was supposed to know. He's simply that kind of a person, a narcissistic person. Upon seeing that, I went back to Banja Luka, and I remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Before we move on to your return to Banja Luka, let's get back to Omarska Camp and what you observed them, and then we'll move on to that issue. Where you observed these bodies on the second floor, was that the room where these triages were conducting interrogations?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In those premises where I was up on that floor, the people who were brought there were people who were under investigation. There was an operative procedure in place against them, and people were questioned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the former SNB chief who you spoke with, can you give us his name?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given what he's like as a person, and also given that he himself was hurt by everything that was going on at Keraterm and Omarska, I would kindly like to ask the Court to give that name, if absolutely necessary, in a private session because I would rather not utter it publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you were at Omarska Camp, did you have the opportunity to observe who was guarding the camp?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Omarska, I saw at the gates members of the public security service; but to tell you the truth, it's a rather large perimeter. And then inside I saw numerous members of military formations of the Army of Republika Srpska. I can't tell you whether they also had a role in securing the camp. I really wouldn't be able to tell you because the perimeter is rather large.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any women, elderly, or children at the camp that day?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Omarska Camp, I did not have occasion to see them. I saw them at Trnopolje. At Trnopolje, I saw many children, women, the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you visited Trnopolje Camp that day as well?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Prosecutor, I said already what was the reason for me going to those places, to the collection centre. As I have said to you, I wanted to establish which of our collaborators, who had been our collaborators before the conflict broke out, were located there in order to allow them to get in touch with their relatives and to also have a choice in deciding where would they go, et cetera. It was my duty to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now let's talk about your return to Banja Luka that day. When you returned to Banja Luka, what happened? Did you meet with your superiors?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, is this going to be a very short answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I was looking at this clock, but you're right, the one on the computer is different, and so, yes, we should stop here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radulovic, your testimony is -- you're completed day 2 of your testimony. We are not going to rise immediately. We have a procedural matter we wish to deal with. So the usher will escort you from the courtroom. We will reconvene tomorrow in a different courtroom. And you would remember the cautions I gave you yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And before I hear from Mr. Pantelic, I should alert you, Mr. Olmsted, that you have used five hours and forty minutes, so you would have, if my arithmetic is correct, two hours and twenty minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can I address that after -- that issue just briefly? We can do Mr. Pantelic first, and then I can just raise a couple issues with regard to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you, being grateful for this time. Your Honours, my learned friend Ms. Korner made a submission last Friday, May 21st. Her submission is on page 10697, line 17, with regard to Traynor's -- Mr. Traynor's articles issue. And she mentioned that I made a submission on May 18th, and the page -- transcript page is 10454, saying that, in fact, I was not objecting to the OTP's position regarding the admission of articles. Unfortunately, as usual, our friends from Prosecution -- maybe it's a lack of professional diligence or I don't know what, they are -- they are trying to misinterpret the situation. In fact, I said, on page 10454, line 22, that I'm ready and I will not object to the admission of Mr. Traynor's article, but only the article in which he was mentioning events where Serbs were victims. Yes, I must admit that it was, to some extent, in ironic way, because obviously Mr. Traynor did not make any particular article with regard to the Serb victims and atrocities against Serbs. So having that in mind, I think that I could have an, at least, apology from Ms. Korner for this misinterpretation of my submission because it was really not only out of context, but it was completely fabricated, sort of say, because transcript is very clear. With regard to Mr. Traynor's article, I want to put on the record that position of Zupljanin Defence is the following: Our understanding is that actually newspaper articles are a form of a creation by journalists of certain events. This is a creative work, and it is nothing to do with hearsay issue. In particular case, Mr. Traynor was very welcome to give his testimony before this Trial Chamber, to testify about his own personal impressions or facts that he was eye-witness or fact witness, and nothing to do with the principle of hearsay through newspaper articles, because we all know how an article can be created and what is the nature of that newspaper article. This is a creative work; this is art to some extent. And that's why we strongly object to the admission of these four proposed articles in relation to my client, Mr. Zupljanin, and these 65 ter numbers are 3378, 3375, 10358.07, and 3373. When reading these four articles, actually, we can conclude how level of interpretation and, I would say, a creative approach was made, not to mention the titles and the headlines in these articles. So I have impression that you already ruled in terms of issue of reconsideration, Your Honours, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Provisionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, but, I mean, that's my impression. I'm just waiting for your final ruling. But this is a very serious and, from our point of view, fundamental issue in relation to the legal aspects of this particular case, and we are very in favour to ask for the certification if your ruling will be that these four particular articles in relation to Mr. Zupljanin - I'm not speaking on behalf of Stanisic Defence in this particular case - that we could ask for the certification. Because, as I said, my -- my approach to this particular issue is that I don't want to create in this particular trial an overall library of articles and materials. We have to be focused - this is a criminal trial - to facts, to eye-witnesses, et cetera. Otherwise, as I said, on one article like this, we could tomorrow, on the same basis, find three or four and five, and where is the end of this story? Just that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, this is taking a little longer than we had thought. And, incidentally, according to the transcript at line 21 of the previous page, I'm recorded as saying "Mr. Pantelic." What I said was "provisionally." In other words, we provisionally ruled on the matter, but obviously we're going to have to take this up tomorrow. So it's past time for the adjournment now, and we would be --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just mention, I'm not proposing to dignify this with a response at the moment. You'll recall last week Mr. O'Sullivan, without any prior notice, got up and made a legal submission. I then asked Your Honour to make an order that if legal submissions are going to be made, we be notified in response, and your response was that you couldn't imagine that that wasn't something that most counsel would do. I was unaware, until Your Honours mentioned it, that Mr. Pantelic was going to raise anything. In spite my request for information via e-mail, I got no answer until 30 seconds ago. Your Honours, I'm now having, unfortunately, to ask that when the Defence are going to making submissions, they notify us in advance. And that's all I want to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we resume tomorrow morning at Courtroom II at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was a request for a ruling at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 27th day of May, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
